The author proposes if the Fourteenth Amendment means that the children of undocumented immigrants are not citizens, as Donald Trump suggests, then they are also not subject to American laws. He needs to lay off the pipe.

That's kinda how the amendment reads, that if you're going to argue that they're not citizens, they must also not be subject to the law.

You could argue this is the only thing keeping diplomats kids from having citizenship if they are born here, as they aren't subject to our laws. It's kinda weird though, that different countries can give out citizenship different ways.

As an example, it's illegal under international law for a child to be stateless, but what if they're born in a country that doesn't do birthright while they're parents are from a country that only does birthright? Under both countries laws, they would be stateless.
Children of diplomats and children of illegal immigrants are not the same thing. And bugger international law, we are a sovereign nation.

He conveniently ignores a lot of the stuff in the National Review article he cites. Especially that there's a difference between "owing allegiance to the US" and "being subject to the laws of the US" in the 14th Amendment's language.

Indeed, during debate over the amendment, Senator Jacob Howard, the author of the citizenship clause, attempted to assure skeptical colleagues that the language was not intended to make Indians citizens of the United States. Indians, Howard conceded, were born within the nation’s geographical limits, but he steadfastly maintained that they were not subject to its jurisdiction because they owed allegiance to their tribes and not to the U.S. Senator Lyman Trumbull, chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, supported this view, arguing that “subject to the jurisdiction thereof” meant “not owing allegiance to anybody else and being subject to the complete jurisdiction of the United States.

Jurisdiction understood as allegiance, Senator Howard explained, excludes not only Indians but “persons born in the United States who are foreigners, aliens, [or] who belong to the families of ambassadors or foreign ministers.” Thus, “subject to the jurisdiction” does not simply mean, as is commonly thought today, subject to American laws or courts. It means owing exclusive political allegiance to the U.S.

His comment about Indians not being culpable in US courts for committing crimes on US soil isn't cited and his quote from Trumbull isn't clear if he's talking about being able to sue Indians in the in the US for acts committed in the US or being able to sue Indians in US courts for acts not committed in the US. Obviously there's a huge difference: of course US courts couldn't exercise jurisdiction over a non-citizen that's not on US soil for an act not committed on US soil. Plus Trumbull uses the term "complete jurisdiction" which probably means the US would still exercise some jurisdiction over foreigners, probably under the territorial principle, which says national courts exercise jurisdiction over events that happen on their soil regardless of the actor's citizenship. In any event, that principle exists today for foreigners in the US.

The National Review article also brings up the fact that Wong Kim Ark was born to parents legally in the US.

I'm not taking a position on this, but the author of the Atlantic article doesn't really make a good case and his little narrative is just silly.
